title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We train LLM alignment auditors with reinforcement learning. In our training environment, the policy investigates target models with hidden behaviors planted in their system prompt. After finetuning Haiku 4.5 on this environment, it matches Opus 4.6 on held-out evaluations for auditing quality and generalizes to harder, fine-tuned targets in a different scaffold.

title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
abstract: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] .

title: Our approach to working with AI companies
abstract: This blog post explains how we approach working with AI companies on projects that the public might rely on to understand risks. It was published on Oct 14, 2026, and we expect to update it over time. At METR, we gather and publish evidence about whether humans could lose control of AI agents on a large scale. We work with AI companies to conduct evaluations, assessments, and investigations, 1 and to share this evidence publicly. As we have seen increasing expectations for these kinds of voluntary engagements to provide external ‘safety assurance’, we want to explain our perspective. In this post, we clarify our overall goals for this work, our approach , and what our approach looks like in practice .

title: How an assessor could investigate control and monitoring of internal AI agents
abstract: Control assessments study whether AI developers’ agents could get away with serious harm without being stopped by the developer’s security and oversight measures. Currently, developers rely heavily on monitors to catch potentially harmful AI behaviors. Here, we discuss how an assessor could collect evidence about the reliability of monitoring. title: A proposal for better informing the public about loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development
abstract: At METR, we aim to give the public evidence about whether frontier AI developers could come to lose control of their internal AI systems. Recent incidents across several AI developers, 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 like the hundreds of rogue agents that broke containment and hacked Hugging Face to hide evidence of cheating from their grader , have raised concerns about the ability of frontier developers to understand and control their internal models, especially as they rapidly become more capable. 9 The public currently lacks the visibility into the internal development of frontier AI systems to tell if these concerns are being addressed, or whether much worse incidents could happen in the near future. We believe closing this public evidence gap is an urgent priority, to allow the public to notice and respond if risks from further development become acute.

title: How an assessor could investigate alignment of unreleased AI models
abstract: AI developers and the public want to know whether AI agents would pursue very harmful actions, like unsanctioned cyberattacks. An alignment assessment would attempt to understand the worst misaligned actions a developer’s agents might pursue in plausible future situations. This would involve: A review of serious misaligned behaviors from all near-frontier internal models observed across training, evaluation, and internal use. An assessment of reasons why the observed behaviors might not be representative of the worst misaligned actions the developer’s agents would take in plausible future situations. This would include: An assessment of whether alignment evals and counterfactual simulations indicate the developer’s agents might take much worse actions under plausible alternative circumstances (although evaluation awareness will likely limit how much the assessor can rely on this evidence).

title: How an assessor could investigate evidence of acceleration from the automation of AI R&D
abstract: This article discusses how an assessor could study whether capabilities progress could accelerate dramatically due to AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D. Such an assessment would answer: Capabilities Progress : How fast are internal capabilities improving, and how much has this progress accelerated recently? Acceleration from AI : If there is an acceleration, how much was it driven by AI automation versus other factors? Bottlenecks to Future Growth : Are there important bottlenecks that could slow growth or limit acceleration in the near term? Limitations : Would these methods reliably identify much more dramatic acceleration if it had occurred? Assessing this would involve analyzing capabilities of unreleased models, understanding the growth of key AI R&D inputs (labor, compute, data, and algorithms), and talking openly with relevant researchers about how AI is impacting their work. title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
abstract: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency.

title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
abstract: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators.

title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
abstract: Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier (rather than pausing outright or failing to coordinate). What should the standard of pacing be? My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately [1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models. You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing [2] . With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on". This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques. Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation.

title: ″[Paper] Distillation for Incrimination and Distillation for Capabilities” by Sebastian Prasanna, Alek Westover
abstract: Subtitle: Empirical work on the Distillation Double Bind. TL;DR: We previously motivated two complementary ways to use distillation for AI safety; we’re releasing a paper empirically testing those ideas. Distillation for Incrimination (DFI) distills an untrusted model into a weaker, trusted one, aiming to transfer the teacher's misalignment but not its ability to hide it, so that auditing the student can incriminate the teacher. We test DFI on AuditBench's secret-keeping model organisms, each fine-tuned to have a hidden quirk and trained to deny it. Distilling them back into their underlying instruction-tuned model yields students that admit the quirk far more often than the organisms do, suggesting that the quirk transferred faster than the propensity to hide it.
